lead.t: Bronchiectasis is permanent, abnormal dilatation of the bronchi with chronic inflammation and infection, leading to a clinical syndrome of chronic productive cough, recurrent chest infections and sometimes haemoptysis.

b: Permanent dilation of bronchi and bronchioles caused by the destruction of smooth muscle and elastic tissue. It typically results from or is associated with chronic necrotizing infections.
Bronchiectasis is not a primary disorder but is always secondary to persistent infection or obstruction.
Bronchial obstruction : Caused by tumors, foreign bodies, or mucus impaction. It also complicates asthma and chronic bronchitis.
Cystic fibrosis : Leads to widespread severe bronchiectasis due to obstruction by viscid mucus and secondary infections.
Immunodeficiency states (especially immunoglobulin deficiencies): Result in recurrent bacterial infections.
Definition: Permanent bronchial dilation from destruction of muscle and elastic tissue due to chronic necrotizing infections
Associations: Cystic fibrosis, Kartagener syndrome, bronchial obstruction

snip.t: Bronchiectasis is permanent, abnormal dilatation of the bronchi with chronic inflammation and infection, leading to a clinical syndrome of chronic productive cough, recurrent chest infections and sometimes haemoptysis.

Parapneumonic effusion and empyema, lung abscess, sepsis and septic shock, respiratory failure and ARDS, pleurisy, pericarditis, lobar collapse, metastatic infection (meningitis, endocarditis, arthritis), bronchiectasis (long term).
Differential: COPD, heart failure ("cardiac asthma"), GORD, vocal cord dysfunction, bronchiectasis, foreign body, PE.

| Bronchiectasis | Chronic wet cough, recurrent sputum‑producing infections, clubbing, localized crackles | High‑resolution CT shows dilated airways with signet‑ring appearance; sputum culture often positive |
Exclude TB, bronchiectasis, cancer and asthma in a patient with chronic cough.

| Bronchiectasis | Chronic daily sputum, frequent infections, hemoptysis, clubbing, history of severe childhood infection | High‑resolution CT shows dilated bronchi with lack of tapering; sputum cultures often polymicrobial |
Congenital and genetic: Cystic fibrosis, primary ciliary dyskinesia (Kartagener: bronchiectasis, sinusitis, dextrocardia), alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, Young's syndrome
Secondary lung abscess: arises on underlying disease: bronchial obstruction (tumour, foreign body), bronchiectasis, septic emboli, TB cavity, pulmonary infarction, immunosuppression.

qs.q: What is the underlying mechanical cause of bronchiectasis?
o: Primary autoimmune destruction of alveolar cells
Permanent bronchial dilation from tissue destruction
Inadequate expansion of air spaces by fluid
Inhaled organic dust leading to hypersensitivity
qs.e: Bronchiectasis is defined as permanent bronchial dilation caused by the destruction of muscle and elastic tissue due to chronic necrotizing infections. Compression atelectasis is what results from pleural fluid collections.

qs.q: What structural alteration defines bronchiectasis among chronic airway disorders?
o: Permanent dilation of bronchi and bronchioles due to tissue destruction
Permanent enlargement of air spaces distal to terminal bronchioles
Localized fibrotic contraction of the pleura restricting expansion
Diffuse granulomatous inflammation involving noncaseating nodules
qs.e: Bronchiectasis involves permanent dilation of bronchi and bronchioles driven by the destruction of their smooth muscle and elastic tissue. Emphysema involves enlargement distal to terminal bronchioles without fibrosis.

qs.q: A 52-year-old non-smoking woman presents with subpleural ground-glass opacities and traction bronchiectasis on HRCT. Histopathology shows uniform interstitial inflammation and fibrosis without honeycombing. What is her expected 5-year survival rate compared to classic IPF?
o: 80%, indicating a better prognosis than classic IPF
50%, which is identical to the prognosis of classic IPF
20%, indicating a much more fulminant clinical course
95%, indicating near-complete spontaneous resolution rate
qs.e: Nonspecific Interstitial Pneumonia (NSIP) has a 5-year survival rate of 80%, offering a significantly better prognosis than idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis. IPF carries a 5-year survival rate of only 50%.

qs.q: A 41-year-old woman has episodic dyspnea with expiratory wheezes, elevated serum IgE, peripheral eosinophilia, sputum eosinophils, perihilar bronchiectasis on CXR, and detectable serum galactomannan. Most likely pathologic finding in her bronchi?
o: Non-invasive aspergillosis
Blastomycosis
Invasive candidiasis
ANCA-associated vasculitis
qs.e: Elevated IgE + eosinophilia + galactomannan (Aspergillus cell wall component) + bronchiectasis + asthma exacerbations = allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA). The fungus colonizes bronchi non-invasively.

qs.q: Bronchiectasis in Kartagener syndrome results from
o: Abnormal chloride transport causing viscid mucus
Immunoglobulin deficiency causing recurrent infections
Structural ciliary abnormalities impairing mucociliary clearance
Chronic aspiration causing repeated necrotizing pneumonia
qs.e: Kartagener syndrome involves structural ciliary abnormalities (autosomal recessive). Impaired mucociliary clearance leads to persistent infections, bronchial wall destruction, and bronchiectasis.

qs.q: A patient with cystic fibrosis develops severe irreversible airway dilation. The pathogenesis of bronchiectasis in this setting involves
o: Immune complex deposition in bronchial walls
Smooth muscle destruction by autoantibodies
Ciliary structural defects impairing clearance
Viscid mucus causing obstruction followed by infection
qs.e: In cystic fibrosis, abnormally viscid mucus causes bronchial obstruction, predisposing to recurrent infections. The combination of obstruction and chronic necrotizing infection leads to irreversible bronchiectasis.

rx.name: Bronchiectasis
first: Daily airway clearance (physiotherapy) is the foundation
Antibiotics for an exacerbation, chosen from the sputum culture: amoxicillin or doxycycline; ciprofloxacin for Pseudomonas; usually 14 days

ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Bronchiectasis is permanent, abnormal dilation of bronchi caused by chronic infection or obstruction, leading to chronic productive cough, recurrent infections, and sometimes haemoptysis.

sections.p: Bronchiectasis is irreversible bronchi dilation due to loss of smooth muscle and elastic tissue from chronic necrotizing infection or obstruction. Diagnosis requires high‑resolution CT showing bronchial wall thickening and a broncho‑arterial ratio >1.
b: HRCT is the gold‑standard imaging test
Diagnostic criteria: broncho‑arterial ratio >1, lack of tapering, or visible bronchial wall within 1 cm of the pleura

sections.p: Severity is graded by symptom burden, exacerbation frequency, lung function, and radiologic extent (e.g., FACED or Bronchiectasis Severity Index).
b: FACED: FEV1, Age, Chronic colonisation, Extent, Dyspnoea
Higher scores predict mortality and guide intensity of follow‑up

sections.p: Bronchiectasis is always secondary. In most settings the leading cause is post‑infectious damage; in low‑resource areas additional causes are common.
b: Post‑infectious (post‑pneumonia, severe childhood infections)
Cystic fibrosis (especially in high‑income settings)
Primary ciliary dyskinesia/Kartagener syndrome
Chronic obstruction (tumour, foreign body, mucus plugging)
Immunodeficiency (IgG deficiency, HIV)
Tuberculosis or post‑TB scarring (important in low‑resource settings)
Non‑tuberculous mycobacteria, especially in COPD

sections.p: Patients develop a chronic productive cough with purulent sputum, recurrent chest infections, and may have haemoptysis or breathlessness on exertion.
b: Daily cough with sputum >3 months
Exacerbations requiring antibiotics
Occasional haemoptysis
Progressive dyspnoea, especially with basal disease

sections.p: Targeted tests confirm the diagnosis, identify causative organisms, and assess severity.

t.b: Does the airway show irreversible dilation? Positive result confirms bronchiectasis; if unavailable, consider chest X‑ray plus clinical picture.
What is the airflow limitation? Reduced FEV1/FVC indicates obstructive physiology; severity guides management.
Which pathogen is colonising? Identifies treatable organisms; negative cultures do not exclude infection.
Is there an underlying immunodeficiency? Low IgG suggests need for replacement therapy.
Is allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis present? Positive results direct steroid therapy.

sections.p: Complications can be life‑threatening and require urgent care.
b: Massive haemoptysis
Severe respiratory failure or hypercapnia
Sepsis from uncontrolled infection
Pneumothorax in advanced disease

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause, reduce bacterial load, and support airway clearance.
b: Antibiotics: long‑term macrolide or inhaled antibiotics for chronic Pseudomonas; avoid quinolones if QT risk high
Airway clearance: chest physiotherapy, oscillatory devices, postural drainage
Bronchodilators for co‑existent asthma/COPD
Vaccinations: influenza, pneumococcal, COVID‑19
Immunoglobulin replacement if IgG deficiency
Surgery (resection) only for localized disease refractory to medical therapy

sections.p: Regular review prevents exacerbations and monitors progression.
b: Clinic review every 6–12 months with spirometry and sputum culture
Prompt treatment of exacerbations to avoid lung damage
Lifestyle: smoking cessation, nutrition optimisation

sections.p: Conditions that share chronic cough and sputum production.
b: COPD (especially chronic bronchitis)
Asthma with mucus hypersecretion
Heart failure (cardiac asthma)
Tuberculosis

sections.p: Some investigations may appear normal despite disease.
b: Chest X‑ray can be normal early; HRCT is needed
Sputum cultures may be negative during stable periods
FEV1 may be preserved in early bronchiectasis

whenToSeekHelp: Fever, chills, and increasing sputum purulence suggesting sepsis

faq.q: Why does bronchiectasis cause a chronic cough?
faq.a: Damaged airways retain mucus, which triggers cough receptors and promotes bacterial growth, perpetuating inflammation.
The airway dilation is irreversible; treatment aims to control infection, improve clearance, and slow progression.
When disease is localized, refractory to medical therapy, and causing severe symptoms or complications.
